title: Assam-Born Scientist Builds Detectors for NASA Telescope That Will Hunt for Life Beyond Earth
excerpt: Dr. Angaraj Duara is developing CMOS image detectors at the Open University for potential use on NASA's Habitable Worlds Observatory, the first large telescope designed to search for life on other worlds.
body:
• Dr. Angaraj Duara, an Assam-born scientist at the Open University in England, is building CMOS image detectors for potential use on NASA's upcoming flagship Habitable Worlds Observatory.
  • The Habitable Worlds Observatory will be NASA's first large space telescope designed specifically to search for signs of life on planets orbiting other stars, aiming to image around 25 potentially habitable worlds.
  • Duara, funded by the UK Space Agency, earned his PhD from the University of Leicester working on detectors for the Cherenkov Telescope Array, the world's largest ground-based gamma-ray observatory.
  • For the diaspora: his path — from Assam to a lead role on a NASA flagship mission via British academia — is a working blueprint for Indian STEM talent abroad.

When NASA's next great space telescope launches to hunt for signs of life on other worlds, its eyes may be built — in part — by a scientist from Assam.

Dr. Angaraj Duara, a Space Detector Scientist at the Centre for Electronic Imaging at the Open University in England, is developing CMOS detectors for their potential application on the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO), NASA's upcoming flagship mission. Funded by the UK Space Agency, his work focuses on the delicate imaging hardware that will let the telescope separate the faint light of an Earth-sized planet from the blinding glare of its parent star.

The mission: NASA's life-hunting telescope

The Habitable Worlds Observatory will be a large ultraviolet-optical-infrared space telescope — the scientific successor to Hubble and Webb — and the first large observatory designed specifically to search for signs of life on potentially habitable planets. NASA's goal is to directly image roughly 25 potentially habitable worlds around nearby Sun-like stars and analyse their atmospheres for molecules that could betray surface conditions — biosignatures.

The mission is still in its design phase, with NASA targeting a launch in the 2040s. Its engineering teams are working through the formidable challenge of building a super-stable telescope with a coronagraph powerful enough to distinguish a tiny rocky planet from a star billions of times brighter. It is precisely that detection chain that Duara's detector work feeds into.

The scientist

Duara earned his PhD from the University of Leicester, working on silicon photomultiplier detectors for the Cherenkov Telescope Array — the largest ground-based gamma-ray observatory in the world. He graduated with first-class honours in MPhys Physics with Astrophysics from Leicester's Department of Physics and Astronomy, and previously worked on detectors for CASTOR, a proposed Canadian Space Agency-led telescope mission with NASA and UK Space Agency participation.

Beyond the lab, he has delivered public lectures and media appearances across the UK and India — including interviews with Leicester BBC — speaking on physics and space exploration, a profile that has made him a visible face of Indian scientific talent in Britain.

Why detectors matter

Finding life on an exoplanet is, at its core, an instrumentation problem. The Habitable Worlds Observatory will not photograph aliens; it will read starlight filtered through alien atmospheres, looking for the chemical fingerprints of habitability and, possibly, biology. Every photon counts, and the detectors must be exquisitely sensitive to the difference between light from a planet's atmosphere and light from the star's blinding surface. CMOS detectors — the same class of sensor in smartphone cameras, engineered to a different universe of precision — are a leading candidate technology.

What this means for the diaspora

Duara's trajectory runs through a familiar diaspora pattern: talent nurtured in India, honed in British universities, now deployed on an American flagship mission with British funding. His public-facing work — lectures, school engagements, media — also shows a second-generation model of science diplomacy, where diaspora scientists carry research home to India even as they build it abroad.

What's next

The Habitable Worlds Observatory remains years from final design, and its detector technologies must clear NASA's technology milestones before the mission's critical reviews later this decade. If the CMOS work passes, Duara's detectors could be flying when humanity takes its first spectroscopic look at another Earth.
